extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, critics, and creators seeking an overview of satire (its definitions, modes, techniques, and social functions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for producing and assessing satirical works across media: definitions, aims, tones, common techniques, modes (Horatian/Juvenalian/Menippean), topical focuses, and social functions. Useful for creators deciding approach and critics assessing satirical effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose as constructive social criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire's greater purpose is often constructive social criticism: using wit to draw attention to particular and wider issues in society and to expose or shame perceived flaws of individuals, corporations, government, or society into improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satirical work should aim beyond mere amusement toward exposing vices, follies, abuses or shortcomings; it need not offer solutions but should illuminate problems and contradictions. Example: Swift's A Modest Proposal uses shocking irony to attack indifference to poverty. Scoring note: stronger satire connects wit to a clear critical target and social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional effect should go beyond laughter (wince/after-taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of satire are such that it must do more than make you laugh; no matter how amusing it is, it doesn't count unless you find yourself wincing a little even as you chuckle. Laughter is not an essential component; some satire is not meant to be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire often produces discomfort, a 'serious after‑taste', or cognitive dissonance. Anti-pattern: purely entertaining jokes with no critical bite or consequence; such pieces may be humorous but not satirical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominent use of irony and/or sarcasm
rubrics_metrics.description: A prominent feature of satire is strong irony or sarcasm — 'in satire, irony is militant' — often professing to approve of what it actually criticizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ irony/sarcasm to invert or mock the target's stated values or actions. Guidance: irony should clarify rather than obscure the critique; excessive obliqueness can lose the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment of recognised satirical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire frequently uses parody, burlesque, exaggeration, juxtaposition, comparison, analogy, double entendre, and related devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select devices that amplify the target's folly—e.g., parody imitates to expose, exaggeration magnifies absurdity. Combine devices for effect (juxtaposition + exaggeration). Anti-pattern: relying on a device (e.g., parody) without a clear critical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral/subversive dimension (targets power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire typically has a subversive character and a moral dimension which draws judgment against its targets, often challenging leaders and authorities rather than merely mocking surface features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim satire at conduct, ideology, or power structures rather than only at superficial characteristics. Scoring: satire that undermines perceived authority or exposes systemic flaws scores higher than mere personal insults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from teasing/sfottò
rubrics_metrics.description: Teasing (sfottò) is parodying surface attributes and humanizes targets; by contrast, real satire touches core issues, judges conduct/ideology/power, and seeks to subvert or criticize rather than to humanize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reducing satirical intent to affectionate teasing; ensure critiques address substantive behavior or institutional problems. Anti-pattern: impersonations or mockery that only mimic mannerisms without systemic critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational test of impact (Fo's criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dario Fo's operational criterion: real satire arouses an outraged and violent reaction; the more those in power try to stop you, the better the job you are doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure success partly by resistance from targets or authorities (censorship, public outrage). Caveat: censorship as success signal is context-dependent and ethically fraught; risk assessment required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode: Horatian (tone and aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horatian satire playfully criticises social vice through gentle, mild, light-hearted humour; the goal is to chide and 'heal with smiles' rather than to attack harshly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gentle wit, self-deprecation, and sympathetic tone when the aim is mild correction. Appropriate for targets where ridicule should be temperate. Anti-pattern: applying Horatian tone to issues requiring harsher moral indictment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode: Juvenalian (tone and aim)
rubrics_metrics.description: Juvenalian satire is contemptuous, abrasive, and characterized by sarcasm, moral indignation and personal invective; it attacks perceived social evil and often aims to provoke change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a scornful, serious tone when targeting corruption or systemic evil; humour may be less central. Risk: can alienate audiences; ensure ground for moral outrage is clear and defensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode: Menippean (form and mixture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Menippean satire mixes seriousness and mockery (diatribe, dialogue, parodies) and often blends genres and tones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Menippean form when you want to combine philosophical critique, parody, and varied narrative devices. Expect complexity; clarity of intent helps prevent confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate topical focus (politics, religion, sex, manners)
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire commonly targets politics (pre‑eminent), religion, sex, and manners; topics are often taboo and thus effective for satiric exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose topic aligned with intended critique and audience. Recognize sensitivities (taboos) and legal/cultural risks. Scoring: topical, timely satire often has higher impact (e.g., political satire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone selection across a spectrum
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire's tones span wit, ridicule, irony, sarcasm, cynicism, the sardonic, and invective; choice of tone shapes intent and reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone to mode and target (Horatian → witty; Juvenalian → invective). Avoid tonal mismatch (e.g., sardonic tone on light-hearted subject) that undermines credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of grotesque, scatology, and black humour when purposeful
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque and scatological elements (including scatology symbolizing corruption) and black/gallows humour have long associations with satire and can emphasize disgust or deadness in a target.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ such elements to symbolize moral rot or to shock into awareness, not gratuitously. Anti-pattern: gratuitous obscenity that distracts from critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and form suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Satire appears across many media (internet memes, literature, plays, commentary, music, film, television, cartoons, stand-up); form choice affects methods and reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a medium that amplifies the chosen devices and reaches the intended audience (e.g., political cartoons for visual irony; long-form prose for complex diatribes). Consider constraints (length, format conventions) when designing satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social and political context sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of political satire in a society reflects tolerance levels; under totalitarian regimes satire may be suppressed and adapt (anecdotes, indirect forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess legal and cultural context for safety and effectiveness; in repressive contexts prefer indirect or coded forms. Success metrics should account for both impact and risk.
